extracted.intended_audience: reporters and journalism students who cover political beats / newsroom reporters
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for reporters on gathering, writing, and editing political news — how to research background, handle sources, maintain fairness, and produce copy for campaigns, conventions and local politics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use interpretation sparingly; avoid premature forecasting
rubrics_metrics.description: Political reporting should be objective and exact like other news until information becomes complicated; interpretation (especially forecasting) should be used sparingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporters are warned not to interpret before learning enough to analyze; forecasting politics is risky (many experienced political analysts guess wrong) and should be avoided whenever possible. "He fears that a 'straight news' political story brands him as a greenhorn. Actually, it marks him as sensible and discerning."

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish forecasts from retrospective interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Draw a sharp line between interpretation that forecasts future events and interpretation that looks backward to explain how the present situation developed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retrospective interpretation that shows how current conditions arose can be justified; prediction-style interpretation is much more hazardous (example: Delphic two-way answers). Use the former when warranted, avoid the latter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circulate among politicians of all parties to build background
rubrics_metrics.description: Spend time with politicians great and small, frequent party headquarters and other political gathering places to learn speech, habits of thinking, history and reputation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporter must know politicians personally so they will talk and answer questions. Background is built by incessant contact and vigorous study of newspaper files — you can't become expert from six or seven speeches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know which politicians are influential
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify which politicians actually wield influence (which may not correspond to official position).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The mayor may be a figurehead while a back-stager who holds no office does the real work. Reporter must discover local power dynamics and unexpected influential actors (example: Frank Cluett as precinct dictator).

rubrics_metrics.name: Know which politicians give accurate and sensible explanations
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine which sources can provide reliable analysis and sensible interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This involves understanding human nature and balancing your own estimate with others' views; the shrewdest analyst may be outside active politics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know which politicians you can trust
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish trustworthy sources from those who will use the reporter as a megaphone for falsehoods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Until trust is established, reporters are at the mercy of politicians who may give false 'explanations' that will be printed; learning who can be trusted is essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know the local political history and past issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Learn past issues, how they were decided, what current issues may be, and factors likely to settle them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study files and history thoroughly; examples include motives behind a mayor's announced actions and coalition dynamics. This is essential context to avoid misjudging events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand each party's machine and how it works
rubrics_metrics.description: Learn party organization, bases of support, ward/precinct structures, and local political monarchs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Know how machines capture votes (factory-worker, religious, ethnic appeals). Understanding ward and precinct power is critical (e.g., precinct bosses).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use books and newspaper archives; don't rely on a few speeches
rubrics_metrics.description: Supplement reporting with reading (e.g., recommended Frank R. Kent) and thorough study of earlier newspaper files.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One book can give 'the feel' of politics and speed a reporter's ripening; do not assume expertise after a handful of speeches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate trust so off-the-record and candid information flows
rubrics_metrics.description: When trusted, political leaders will speak freely, often providing off-the-record information that can be attributed to 'well-informed circles.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat off-the-record material appropriately and recognize that even reckless politicians will sometimes speak bluntly and honestly when they trust you; being well informed gains access and better coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Watch the general public as well as the professionals
rubrics_metrics.description: Gauge public sentiment and not only political insiders' views, because the public may be shifting away from professionals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporter should sniff faint insurgencies earlier than professionals; circulation wholly among professionals risks missing public shifts (may signal a changing year for a party).

rubrics_metrics.name: Be known as unbiased and fair in all political lairs
rubrics_metrics.description: Regardless of personal beliefs, build a reputation in each party's circles as neutral, fair and not partisan.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid appealing to sources on the basis of shared party identity; being labeled a partisan (e.g., 'Republicrat stooge') can kill access. Maintain perceived neutrality to sustain contacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep news columns neutral; separate news from editorial
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not write partisan or editorialized news copy — the news department must remain neutral even if the editorial page prefers a party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid partisan descriptors and comparisons in news copy (examples of unacceptable biased wording are provided). Most papers hide their political hue on the news pages; learn this and write accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain perspective; don't inflate sideshow candidates
rubrics_metrics.description: Present colorful or theatrical candidates as what they are — entertainment rather than substantive political actors until they prove otherwise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not build up a sideshow performer into a prophet by overenthusiastic coverage; holding charlatans down until they become genuine influences is prudent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present both sides promptly; combine accusation and denial in one story
rubrics_metrics.description: When a candidate levels accusations, hustle to obtain the opponent's immediate reply so the story presents attack and defense together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Running attack alone and leaving reply for a later story is unfair; combine both in one story to prevent lies from gaining unchallenged traction. Example story shows accusation followed immediately by Grady's explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be mindful of libel law when publishing political attacks
rubrics_metrics.description: Understand that false statements may be libelous even when made at political rallies, and that a candidate can sue at any time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some cities accept statements at rallies as usable unless they involve direct immorality, but reporters should not rely on that understanding. If deleting libelous statements distorts the story, include the defense concurrently to be fair.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt newsroom rules limiting last-minute personal attacks before elections
rubrics_metrics.description: Many papers prohibit personal attacks later than the Sunday before election to prevent last-minute mudslinging without opportunity to reply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such a rule decreases late dirty campaigning; if attacks must run over weekend, the opponent has Monday to reply. It's recommended that reporters adopt this rule; politicians complain at first but accept it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require opportunity to reply before printing personal attacks
rubrics_metrics.description: Some offices enforce no personal attacks (well-founded or false) printed until the subject has had an opportunity to answer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This stricter rule is 'splendid' but harder to enforce than the 'not after Sunday' rule; unanswered attacks may be printed only if the subject refuses to answer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't ban all attacks unconditionally; use careful judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Eliminating all personal attacks can be purity carried too far, because some attacks are valid and deleting them protects wrongdoing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determining where battles can go when they switch from issues to personalities requires sober and careful judgment — balance fairness against public interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Level coverage lengths to avoid appearance of favoritism
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid grossly unequal story lengths for candidates when news values would give one much more copy than another, because readers will suspect boosting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If one candidate's speeches are far more quotable, consider extending the weaker candidate's copy to similar length to preserve reputation for fairness; make-up editors may protest, but fairness to readers is paramount.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be ready to reallocate space when minor contests gain importance
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjust news values and space allocation when an expected minor contest begins to dominate public attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Increase coverage of races (e.g., library trustees) as they build momentum; do not needle them but grant more space when warranted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid campaign-speech language and overworked diction
rubrics_metrics.description: Write in newspaper language, not campaign-speech bromides and clichés that repeat the same handful of phrasings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watch for stories full of bromides that 'reek like a drugstore' and remind yourself to avoid reusing political phraseology (example 'battle royal', 'war horses', 'girded for the fray').

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand primary-time insurrections are often ritualistic
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that many primary-era challenges and 'independence' declarations are temporary maneuvers that do not reflect lasting party schisms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Candidates who 'jump off the reservation' during primaries often return to the machine after defeat; reporter should interpret primary insurrections in context and not overstate their significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand why parties run lost-cause candidates
rubrics_metrics.description: Know that parties sometimes field prominent but unwanted candidates to satisfy internal pressures or reward service while shielding preferred leaders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties may run a flattering but politically expendable candidate (e.g., to satisfy a restless local figure) while protecting core leaders from exposure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize organizational advantage over independents
rubrics_metrics.description: Understand that party organization and machine strength usually overwhelm independent or 'sticker' candidates despite the independent's superior ability or message.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unless independents build comparable organization, thorough party precinct-by-precinct machinery will corral votes; independents win occasionally but are typically handicapped by lack of machine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overemphasizing racial/ethnic explanations for tickets
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not automatically interpret each ticket as arranged solely for ethnic or racial group appeals; overdoing this thesis is socially harmful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid framing candidates primarily as ethnic appeals (Irish, French, Italian, etc.) since this encourages division and keeps groups separate; consider merit and other reasons for selections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not become cynical; avoid jaundiced portrayal of politics
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain an open mind and avoid a permanently suspicious or jaundiced view that discourages public participation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remember that despite abuses, the American system is preferable to dictatorships; cynical reporting can keep readers away from the polls and undermine democratic corrective mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider broader audience (county/rural readers) when covering regional politics
rubrics_metrics.description: When reporting county politics, remember readers include town and rural people whose concerns and loyalties may differ from city dwellers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate candidates' local histories and ties (e.g., former postmaster in a district) that explain regional voting shifts; adapt coverage to varied audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare convention reporting with delegate lists and organized check-off procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: For conventions, obtain a complete alphabetical list of delegates/districts and check off votes as reported to keep an accurate running count.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrange helpers to hurry fragments of information to telephones; assign a dedicated telephone and assistants so information reaches the office promptly — don't try to do the whole job alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid premature trend leads; don't predict final convention results from early counts
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not assume early leads are decisive in small delegate pools; a few changing delegates can overturn apparent leads.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resist writing a 'Lead Convention' based on halfway counts when the total vote is small enough for late shifts to change the outcome; it's safer not to risk premature conclusions.
